summary: This informational memo describes how ICPv2 from RFC 2186 is applied to web caching.

plainLanguage.summary: A guide on how neighboring caches use their questions to save time.

questions: how to use icp with web caches
what is icp internet cache protocol
what is the difference between a parent and sibling cache
subtitle: How Web caches use ICPv2 to ask their neighbors who already has a page, and what went wrong along the way.

tldr.problem: Groups of Web caches can save traffic by sharing, but RFC 2186 only defines the ICP message format. Implementers needed a record of how ICP is actually used in practice.
tldr.mechanism: A cache that misses sends ICP queries over UDP to its parent and sibling caches, collects HIT or MISS replies, and then fetches the object from the best source. The RFC documents each step as the Harvest and Squid caches perform it.
tldr.outcome: The memo is informational. It also lists design flaws of ICPv2 and security weaknesses, such as spoofed replies, and discourages the ICP_OP_HIT_OBJ feature.

today: RFC 2187 is an Informational memo with no recorded replacement or update, and it describes Harvest 1.4pl2 and Squid 1.1.10 as they were in September 1997. The message format it relies on is in RFC 2186.

sections.title: Why This Memo Exists
sections.content:
ICP (Internet Cache Protocol) is a lightweight message format that Web caches use to exchange hints about whether a URL is held in a neighbor cache. The message format itself is in the companion document, RFC 2186. This memo describes how ICP is applied in software.

The authors say they document practice rather than judge it. ICP may be a net win in some situations and a net loss in others, and some practices described are suboptimal. The memo does still address known security problems and shortcomings. ICP was first developed at the University of Southern California as a central part of hierarchical caching in the Harvest research project.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a guidebook about how caches ask each other for pages. It tells what people actually do, not what they should do.

sections.title: Cache Hierarchies: Parents and Siblings
sections.content:
In a cache hierarchy (or mesh), a cache sets up peering relationships with neighbor caches. There are two kinds: a parent is one level up, and a sibling is on the same level. When a cache does not hold an object, it may ask its neighbors over ICP. A neighbor hit can be fetched from a parent or a sibling. A neighbor miss may be fetched from a parent, but may not be fetched from a sibling.

So a parent provides transit for any request, while a sibling only serves what it already has cached. The hierarchy also tries to avoid choke points: a neighbor can be restricted to certain DNS domains, and only cachable requests are forwarded. Requests that are inherently uncachable, such as those needing certain types of authentication or highly personalized responses, should be handled directly by lower-level caches.

The added value of ICP is that without it (or something similar) sibling relationships are not possible, since there would be no way to ask nearby caches about a document. ICP replies also show whether a neighbor is reachable, and because an idle cache answers faster than a busy one, they give a form of load balancing. The extra query delay may be more than offset by faster delivery from a neighbor.
sections.plainLanguage: A parent is like a big sister who will go and find anything for you. A sibling is like a friend who will only hand you things they already have.

sections.title: The ICP Query and Reply Steps
sections.content:
The basic sequence has four steps: the local cache receives an HTTP request from a client, sends ICP queries, the peers reply, and the local cache decides where to forward the request. The descriptions follow Harvest version 1.4pl2 and Squid version 1.1.10.

A request produces ICP traffic only if it is not a cache hit, not for a local server, is a GET request, and does not match the hierarchy_stoplist. By default the cache sends an ICP_OP_QUERY to each peer, except where domain restrictions apply, where the peer is a sibling and the request has Pragma: no-cache, or where the peer is set to no-query. It expects a reply from each peer that is believed up, and installs a timeout, two seconds by default in Squid and Harvest. A peer is marked down after it fails to reply to 20 consecutive queries.

The receiver tests its reply in this order: ICP_OP_ERR if the URL cannot be parsed, ICP_OP_DENIED if access controls forbid the peer, ICP_OP_HIT if the object is cached and fresh for at least the next 30 seconds, then ICP_OP_MISS_NOFETCH if it does not want the peer to fetch from it, and finally ICP_OP_MISS by default. An ICP_OP_HIT_OBJ reply carries the object itself and can be used only if the query had ICP_FLAG_HIT_OBJ set and the whole object fits in an ICP message (maximum 16 Kbytes).

On the querying side, a HIT starts retrieval from that peer at once. Sibling misses are ignored. If all peers miss, the cache picks the peer with the lowest RTT to the origin server when ICP_FLAG_SRC_RTT is in use, otherwise the first parent that missed (FIRST_PARENT_MISS), and otherwise goes straight to the origin server unless a firewall prevents it.
sections.plainLanguage: You shout the question to every neighbor and wait a couple of seconds. The first one who says yes gives you the page. If everyone says no, you ask a parent or go to the source.

sections.title: Configuration Examples
sections.content:
Peering is set up by manual configuration at both ends. The memo uses Squid directives for a customer cache and an ISP cache. The customer writes cache_host cache.isp.com parent 8080 3130, where the type is parent, sibling or multicast, followed by the HTTP port and the ICP port. local_domain keeps local servers out of the hierarchy, and cache_host_domain limits the parent to chosen DNS domains.

The ISP side uses access lists. Allowing the customer through http_access and icp_access makes the ISP cache a parent. To enforce a sibling relationship the ISP adds miss_access deny for the customer. The relationship type is never carried in the ICP query itself, so the ISP should also tell the customer to configure it as a sibling.
sections.plainLanguage: Two caches have to agree by hand on who is the parent and who is the sibling. Nothing in the message says so.

sections.title: Firewalls and Multicast
sections.content:
A cache behind a firewall cannot always reach origin servers. Harvest and Squid have an inside_firewall directive that lists the domains on the near side. With a single parent on the firewall itself there is no need for ICP. With several peers behind the firewall, ICP can still find hits, and if no replies arrive the cache must pick a parent instead of going direct.

A cache may also send ICP queries to a multicast address that neighbors join. Replies are sent only by unicast. The memo gives three reasons: multicasting replies would not reduce the number of packets, it avoids unexpected replies to other group members, and the reply should follow the unicast path that the later HTTP request will take. Caches should ignore ICP messages from addresses not configured as neighbors, and use the minimum multicast TTL needed. Because the number of multicast replies is unknown, Squid sends a test query every 15 minutes and uses a moving average, rounded down.
sections.plainLanguage: Shouting to a whole room is quick, but anyone can join the room. So you only listen to the people you already know.

sections.title: Lessons Learned and Design Flaws
sections.content:
ICP is deliberately simple: a fixed binary header, and the only thing it shares with HTTP is the URL. It has no field for the request method, so it cannot handle non-GET requests, and it cannot express Pragma: no-cache, If-Modified-Since or the HTTP/1.1 Cache-Control features. For this reason the memo discourages ICP_OP_HIT_OBJ.

ICP also says nothing about whether two caches are parent or sibling, so the querying cache must apply HIT or MISS to its own configuration. The memo contrasts ICP as an object-location hint with ICP being used to convey cache usage policy, which needs a very accurate prediction of the later HTTP result.

Listed flaws of ICPv2 include the NULL-terminated URL in the payload, IPv4-specific Sender and Requester Host Address fields that are normally zero-filled, options limited to 32 flags and 32 bits of data, the URL no longer being an adequate cache key, different opcodes for query and response, and no authentication fields.

On security, ICP over UDP is open to IP address spoofing. Bogus replies can stop a neighbor being used or force it to be used, and a spoofed ICP_OP_HIT_OBJ could pollute a cache with invalid objects. Multicast queries let others eavesdrop on URLs. The memo suggests the IP Authentication Header and ESP underneath ICP.
sections.plainLanguage: The first version was made very small and simple, so it cannot say everything a web request can. The authors list what they would fix next time.
